what: Scotch yoke. One motor turns a 16 mm crank. Its offset pin carries a block captured in a guide across a yoke. The block slides transversely while separate longitudinal guides keep the yoke from rotating. Watch the blue unmotorized yoke move through a 32 mm stroke, slow to zero speed at each end, and reverse while the crank keeps turning. The red transverse block is a second observable moving part; neither slider has its own motor. A captured transverse block projects a 16 mm crank circle into two perpendicular 32 mm slider strokes. Compare sinusoidal position, speed, acceleration and reverse return.
try: Select SineShuttle in Examples. The matching program loads into blocks automatically. Reset before each fresh experiment, then press Run. Open Instructions to see all 105 pieces and their assembly steps.

Reset to the saved pose and press Run. Motor A makes one forward turn at 30 degrees per second, then two at 90, then three reverse turns at 90 to return to zero. The program holds for half a second between legs and at the return. A startup guard requires the encoder to be within one degree of its saved datum.

Follow the yoke relative to the frame and the block relative to the yoke. The yoke travels along one axis; the block absorbs the perpendicular component of the crank-pin motion. Check that both move through their useful travel and remain captured in their respective guides.

Compare the slow, fast and reverse passes. Count one full out-and-back stroke for every crank revolution. Measure actual carriage positions and crank phases at the ends and midpoints; an encoder reaching its target does not prove that the yoke moved correctly.

Compare moving intervals away from startup, stopping, correction moves and held pauses. At nearly constant crank speed the two half strokes span the same 180 degrees. The yoke moves fastest at midstroke and is momentarily stationary at each end. Its transverse slider is then moving fastest.
why: The crank pin has two perpendicular coordinates. Choose the longitudinal crank direction as phase zero. Its longitudinal projection is r cosθ, and its transverse projection is r sinθ. The captured block can slide across the yoke but cannot leave that guide. The separate longitudinal guides prevent the yoke rotating, so its position must equal the longitudinal pin coordinate. No finite-length connecting rod adds an angle-dependent correction. Consequently x−xc=r cosθ and q−qc=r sinθ. Here x is yoke position relative to the frame and q is block position relative to the yoke. Each coordinate has a full stroke of 2r and their phases differ by a quarter-turn.
matters: A Scotch yoke converts continuous rotation into harmonic translation through physical constraints. The program controls only the fixed-axis crank; the passive yoke follows the mechanism. Scotch yoke and orthogonal trammel are related inversions of the double-slider chain: which link is fixed and where the drive acts are different. This collection already contains sinusoidal straight-line markers and trammel sliders. The addition here is the captured red block moving across the blue translating yoke, which makes the projection directly visible. Joint play, friction, acceleration and solver error can affect a measured run.
question: The second forward pass runs three times as fast as the first. What happens to the stroke, cycle period, peak yoke speed and ideal peak acceleration? Does zero speed at a stroke end mean the yoke has a finite dwell?
answer: The full stroke remains 32 mm. At constant speed, the period changes from 12 seconds to 4 seconds and the ideal peak speed triples from about 8.38 to 25.13 mm/s. Peak acceleration scales with the square of angular speed, so it becomes nine times larger. The yoke is stationary only at an instant at each ideal stroke end; it does not have a finite dwell while the crank keeps turning. The half-second stops in the supplied program are commanded pauses, not a dwell created by the yoke geometry.
further: Use the actual crank phase to compare the measured yoke and transverse block coordinates with cosine and sine. Both should cover 32 mm peak to peak. The squared centered coordinates satisfy (x−xc)²+(q−qc)²=r² in ideal geometry; estimate residuals from independently measured positions.

Compare Quickstroke. Its offset guide and finite connecting rod produce unequal stroke times. Even a centered slider-crank retains a finite-rod angularity term; equal half-stroke timing alone is not proof of a Scotch yoke.

Compare Circle Splitter or Crossline: their straight sinusoidal marker paths come from geared counterrotation. Ellipsa and Ellipse Engine belong to the same broad double-slider chain family as this yoke. Identify which link is grounded, where the motor sits and which body is observed; these different inversions explain the distinct experiments.

Reverse the motor. The same ideal path is retraced, while the instantaneous direction at a given phase reverses. Return to the saved datum and compare both passive parts with their starting positions. Manual changes or a new radius require a newly checked envelope; reset before rerunning the supplied experiment.
Use the motor override to jog A in 15° steps within 0…1080°. Turn override off and reset before running the complete program.
formula: Ideal geometry: r=40 LDU=16 mm; x−xc=r cosθ; q−qc=r sinθ; stroke=2r=32 mm. At constant angular speed ω in rad/s: vx=−rω sinθ; ax=−rω² cosθ; T=2π/|ω|. At 30°/s: T=12 s, |vx|max=8.37758 mm/s. At 90°/s: T=4 s, |vx|max=25.13274 mm/s. Each constant-speed half stroke takes T/2. In the authored LDraw X/Z plane, θ is measured from +X toward +Z; the saved phase is θ0=0 and the placed motor gives θ=−A for native encoder A. x is the longitudinal X coordinate and q is the block coordinate along authored +Z relative to the yoke. The finite encoder route is 0→360→1080→0 degrees, not a prescribed yoke trajectory.
